pillar_reactions.evidence: 'Yeah' and then, asked whether learning the why would help him keep it going, 'yeah for sure... you teach them one versus, you know, like you just said, we teach them how to fish.' He had already accepted the premise before the pillar was delivered — his stated reason for taking the call was that four sessions of 45 minutes 'obviously fits my lifestyle a lot more' than an hour-plus in a gym.

The only pillar he actively negotiated. Told that calorie counting is not usually part of it, he pushed back with his own history: 'whenever I was at my peak fitness, I actually was calorie counting... I felt like that was what got me to be my most successful, because I knew everything that was going in.' He then argued for it in the first month specifically as a recalibration, while being clear he does not want it permanently — 'it's a pain to get the scale out and weigh this... but I feel like it is one of the ways I know how to be, like, this is what I'm truly getting in my body.' The rep adapted, noted it down and said he would pass it to Trevor.

'No. It sounds good' when asked for questions. He had pre-empted the whole pillar earlier with an unusually direct commitment statement: 'Commitment is not going to be an issue on my end... if you guys tell me you need to do this, I will do it. It will get done.' He asked one practical question about scheduling — whether workouts are prescribed to a fixed time or done whenever in the day — and was satisfied with the answer.

anchors.raw: in my mind, maybe it was like a couple hundred dollars. The high end, maybe it's like sub a thousand.
anchors.note: An order of magnitude below the offer, arrived with, and never tested at any point before an hour of the prospect's time had been spent. He is explicit that it came from the general market — 'there's a lot of personal one-on-one coaches and blah, blah, blah out there. Usually people are in a couple hundred dollar range' — and equally explicit that he is not disputing the value, only his access to it.

anchors.raw: Anecdotally, I have had success counting my calories, lifting weights, running or doing cardio the traditional way. So I know that works.
anchors.note: He has a working method already and says so twice, including the arithmetic — 'it's simple math. My maintenance calories, whatever they are, there are a certain number. As long as I'm expending more than I'm consuming, I will lose some body fat. So that's no mystery.' What he is buying is not knowledge but tolerability: the old method requires an hour and twenty minutes a day he does not have.

anchors.raw: No, no chance. I'm not going to ruin my credit, man, for that, that's, no, there's no chance.
anchors.note: Not an anchor against a competing product but against the entire funding mechanism the offer relies on for prospects without liquid cash. Reinforced immediately: 'I'm not going to take out a loan, no... I could be Jeff Bezos, and I would never do that.' Where liquidity is absent and borrowing is refused on principle, there is nothing left to work with.

unmet_demand.want: Coaching at somewhere between a couple of hundred and a thousand dollars total, which is the whole range he can access for at least the next twelve to sixteen months
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Nothing in the offer occupies that range. The only alternative is a $200/month community tier that drops the one-to-one coaching, which is precisely the part he needs most as a complete kettlebell novice who says he would otherwise be 'picking it up and swinging it all over the place'.

unmet_demand.want: To know the price before booking an hour-long call — 'I would have preferred if you guys at least had something on the website talking about the rate'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: No price appears anywhere in the funnel. The consequence here is measurable on both sides: an unqualifiable prospect took a closer's slot for an hour and left feeling the time was wasted, and the company's stated position is that arriving with the wrong price in mind does not matter.
